title: Intertidal biofilm
wikitext:
{{Short description|Aggregation of microorganisms in low coastline}}
[[File:Biofilm components in streams.jpg|thumb|'''Biofilms in marine environments''' Various biofilm components (including bacteria, algae, and fungi) are embedded in a matrix of extracellular polymeric substances.]]
An '''intertidal bioflim''' is a [[biofilm]] that forms on the [[intertidal]] region of bodies of water. [[Bacteria]] and various [[microorganism]]s, including [[algae]] and [[Fungus|fungi]], form communities of adhered cells called [[biofilm]]s.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=de Carvalho |first=Carla C. C. R. |date=2018 |title=Marine Biofilms: A Successful Microbial Strategy With Economic Implications |journal=Frontiers in Marine Science |volume=5 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2018.00126 |doi-access=free |issn=2296-7745}}</ref> A matrix of [[Extracellular polymeric substance|extracellular polymeric substances (EPS)]] within the biofilm forms sticky coatings on individual [[sediment]] particles and [[Detritus (geology)|detrital]] surfaces.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Decho |first=Alan W |date=2000-07-01 |title=Microbial biofilms in intertidal systems: an overview |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0278434300000224 |journal=Continental Shelf Research |volume=20 |issue=10 |pages=1257–1273 |doi=10.1016/S0278-4343(00)00022-4 |bibcode=2000CSR....20.1257D |issn=0278-4343|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This feature protects bacteria against [[Stress (biology)|environmental stresses]] like temperature and pH fluctuations, UV exposure, changes in salinity, depletion of nutrients, [[antimicrobial|antimicrobial agents]], [[desiccation]], and [[predation]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Particularly, in the ever-changing environments of [[Intertidal zone|intertidal systems]], biofilms can facilitate a range of microbial processes and create protective [[Microenvironment (ecology)|microenvironments]] where cells communicate with each other and regulate further biofilm formation via [[Quorum sensing|Quorum Sensing (QS)]].<ref name=":1" /><sup>,</sup> <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Yung-Hua |last2=Tian |first2=Xiaolin |date=2012-02-23 |title=Quorum Sensing and Bacterial Social Interactions in Biofilms |journal=Sensors |language=en |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=2519–2538 |doi=10.3390/s120302519 |doi-access=free |issn=1424-8220 |pmc=3376616 |pmid=22736963|bibcode=2012Senso..12.2519L }}</ref> While biofilm formation is advantageous to bacteria and other microorganisms involved, the attachment of microorganisms to ship [[Hull (watercraft)|hulls]] can increase fuel consumption and emission of [[greenhouse gas]]es, as well as introduce Non-Indigenous Species (NIS), potentially resulting in harmful economic and ecological impacts on the receiving [[ecosystem]]s.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Cacabelos |first1=Eva |last2=Ramalhosa |first2=Patrício |last3=Canning-Clode |first3=João |last4=Troncoso |first4=Jesús S. |last5=Olabarria |first5=Celia |last6=Delgado |first6=Cristina |last7=Dobretsov |first7=Sergey |last8=Gestoso |first8=Ignacio |date=2020-03-16 |title=The Role of Biofilms Developed under Different Anthropogenic Pressure on Recruitment of Macro-Invertebrates |journal=International Journal of Molecular Sciences |language=en |volume=21 |issue=6 |pages=2030 |doi=10.3390/ijms21062030 |doi-access=free |issn=1422-0067 |pmc=7139543 |pmid=32188145}}</ref>[[File:Biofilm id.JPG|thumb|'''Stages of biofilm development'''   1) Initial Attachment 2) Irreversible Attachment 3) Maturation I 4) Maturation II 5) Dispersion.]]

== Formation and development ==

=== Biofilm formation ===
Biofilm formation begins with the initial attachment of microorganisms to a substrate, such as rocks, shells, or sand in the intertidal zone. This process occurs during the reversible attachment phase, in which the microorganisms only lightly adhere to the substrate.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Stoodley |first1=P. |last2=Sauer |first2=K. |last3=Davies |first3=D. G. |last4=Costerton |first4=J. W. |date=2002-04-19 |title=Biofilms as Complex Differentiated Communities |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.micro.56.012302.160705 |journal=Annual Review of Microbiology |language=en |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=187–209 |doi=10.1146/annurev.micro.56.012302.160705 |pmid=12142477 |issn=0066-4227|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In this phase, the bacteria are encompassed in small amounts of EPS; they are still capable of individual movement and may return to [[plankton]]ic life.<ref name=":2" /><sup>,</sup><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=De Silva |first1=L. A. D. S. |last2=Heo |first2=Gang-Joon |date=2022-12-24 |title=Biofilm formation of pathogenic bacteria isolated from aquatic animals |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00203-022-03332-8 |journal=Archives of Microbiology |language=en |volume=205 |issue=1 |pages=36 |doi=10.1007/s00203-022-03332-8 |pmid=36565346 |issn=1432-072X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Microorganisms may attach to the surface of substrates by weak [[Van der Waals force]]s and [[hydrophobic effect]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Briandet |first1=R |last2=Herry |first2=J. -M |last3=Bellon-Fontaine |first3=M. -N |date=2001-08-01 |title=Determination of the van der Waals, electron donor and electron acceptor surface tension components of static Gram-positive microbial biofilms |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0927776500002137 |journal=Colloids and Surfaces B: Biointerfaces |volume=21 |issue=4 |pages=299–310 |doi=10.1016/S0927-7765(00)00213-7 |pmid=11397632 |issn=0927-7765|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A study of ''[[Pseudomonas aeruginosa]]'' mutants showed that twitching motility by [[Pilus|type IV pili]] contributes to the organism's ability to aggregate on substrates.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=O'Toole |first1=George A. |last2=Kolter |first2=Roberto |date=2002-03-01 |title=Flagellar and twitching motility are necessary for Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm development |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1046/j.1365-2958.1998.01062.x |journal=Molecular Microbiology |language=en |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=295–304 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-2958.1998.01062.x |pmid=9791175 |issn=0950-382X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Another mechanism by which bacteria may adhere to surfaces is the [[Fission (biology)|binary division]] of attached cells.<ref name=":2" />  Similar to colony formation on agar plates, as cells divide, the daughter cells spread expansively, forming cell clusters.<ref name=":2" /> In all cases, adhesion depends on the microorganisms involved, the nature of the substrate, and the chemical and biological conditions of the environment.

The next stage is the irreversible attachment stage, in which microbes start producing EPS. This process creates a three-dimensional polymer network that acts as the biofilm matrix and encloses the bacteria.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Flemming |first1=Hans-Curt |last2=Wingender |first2=Jost |date=2010-09-02 |title=The biofilm matrix |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nrmicro2415 |journal=Nature Reviews Microbiology |language=en |volume=8 |issue=9 |pages=623–633 |doi=10.1038/nrmicro2415 |pmid=20676145 |issn=1740-1534|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In this stage, EPS prevent bacterial cells from moving, keeping them in long-term close contact and allowing interactions such as cell-to-cell communication and [[horizontal gene transfer]] to occur.<ref name=":3" /> In most biofilms, the microbes constitute less than 10% of the dry mass, while the EPS matrix can comprise over 90%.<ref name=":3" />

=== Biofilm development ===

==== Maturation ====
Following the irreversible phase, the next phase of the biofilm life cycle is maturation. In this stage, EPS play a critical role in protecting the biofilm from environmental fluctuations such as [[Oxidative stress|oxidative damage]], antimicrobials, and [[Immune system|host immune system response]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Rather |first1=Muzamil Ahmad |last2=Gupta |first2=Kuldeep |last3=Mandal |first3=Manabendra |date=2021-09-23 |title=Microbial biofilm: formation, architecture, antibiotic resistance, and control strategies |journal=Brazilian Journal of Microbiology |volume=52 |issue=4 |pages=1701–1718 |doi=10.1007/s42770-021-00624-x |issn=1517-8382 |pmc=8578483 |pmid=34558029}}</ref>  Microcolonies are formed as a result of the aggregation of microbial cells and the increase of microbes with accessible nutrients.<ref name=":4" />  With the increase in cells, the biofilm matures and develops into a "tower" or "mushroom" like structure with a complex architecture of fluid-filled channels and pores.<ref name=":2" /><sup>,</sup><ref name=":4" /><sup>,</sup><ref name=":5" />

==== Detachment ====
Detachment, also known as dispersal, is the final stage of the biofilm life cycle. In this stage, cells are released from the biofilm matrix, individually or in clusters, and either resume planktonic life or attach to another surface.<ref name=":2" /><sup>,</sup><ref name=":4" /> Various factors can lead to cell detachment, including insufficient nutrients, competition, lack of oxygen, and environmental factors.<ref name=":5" />

== Features ==

=== Taxonomic diversity ===
Marine biofilm communities have rich and diverse taxa,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Shougang |last2=Su |first2=Xiaoyan |last3=Cui |first3=Han |last4=Wang |first4=Meng |last5=Hu |first5=Xiaoli |last6=Ding |first6=Wei |last7=Zhang |first7=Weipeng |date=2022-06-12 |title=Microbial Richness of Marine Biofilms Revealed by Sequencing Full-Length 16S rRNA Genes |journal=Genes |volume=13 |issue=6 |pages=1050 |doi=10.3390/genes13061050 |doi-access=free |issn=2073-4425 |pmc=9223118 |pmid=35741812}}</ref> with ''[[Cyanobacteria]]'' and ''[[Proteobacteria]]'' being the dominant phyla.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=On On |last2=Chung |first2=Hong Chun |last3=Yang |first3=Jiangke |last4=Wang |first4=Yong |last5=Dash |first5=Swagatika |last6=Wang |first6=Hao |last7=Qian |first7=Pei-Yuan |date=2014-07-09 |title=Molecular techniques revealed highly diverse microbial communities in natural marine biofilms on polystyrene dishes for invertebrate larval settlement |journal=Microbial Ecology |volume=68 |issue=1 |pages=81–93 |doi=10.1007/s00248-013-0348-3 |issn=1432-184X |pmid=24402362|bibcode=2014MicEc..68...81L }}</ref> ''[[Actinobacteria]]'', [[Bacteroidota|''Bacteroidetes'']], and ''[[Planctomycetota|Planctomycetes]]'' are also considered to be dominant phyla but their relative abundances differ between locations.<ref name=":6" /> Site-specific differences also arise within intertidal biofilms. For instance, intertidal biofilms in [[Río de la Plata]] contained high amounts of ''[[Betaproteobacteria]]'' from the ''[[Thauera]]'' genus,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Piccini |first1=C. |last2=García-Alonso |first2=J. |date=2015-02-28 |title=Bacterial diversity patterns of the intertidal biofilm in urban beaches of Río de la Plata |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0025326X14005918 |journal=Marine Pollution Bulletin |series=Marine pollution and assessment of marine status in Latin America |volume=91 |issue=2 |pages=476–482 |doi=10.1016/j.marpolbul.2014.08.039 |pmid=25249253 |bibcode=2015MarPB..91..476P |issn=0025-326X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> whereas intertidal biofilms along the [[Pearl River Delta|Pearl River Estuary]] contained ''[[Alphaproteobacteria]]'' and ''[[Gammaproteobacteria]]'' as the most prominent taxa.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mai |first1=Y. Z. |last2=Peng |first2=S. Y. |last3=Lai |first3=Z. N. |date=2020-01-01 |title=Structural and functional diversity of biofilm bacterial communities along the Pearl River Estuary, South China |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352485518304791 |journal=Regional Studies in Marine Science |volume=33 |article-number=100926 |doi=10.1016/j.rsma.2019.100926 |bibcode=2020RSMS...3300926M |issn=2352-4855|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Extracellular Polymeric Substances (EPS) ===
[[File:Mixed-culture biofilm.jpg|thumb|Scanning electron micrograph of mixed-culture biofilm, showing the arrangement of bacterial cells and extracellular polymeric substances]]
[[Diatom]]s are a major component of intertidal biofilms,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=David J. |last2=Underwood |first2=Graham J. C. |date=2003-12-22 |title=Exopolymer production by intertidal epipelic diatoms |url=https://aslopubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.4319/lo.1998.43.7.1578 |journal=Limnology and Oceanography |language=en |volume=43 |issue=7 |pages=1578–1591 |doi=10.4319/lo.1998.43.7.1578  |doi-access=free|issn=0024-3590|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and they excrete EPS that support many functions, such as desiccation resistance, motility, and [[metabolite]] exchange.<ref name=":7">{{Citation |last1=Underwood |first1=Graham J. C. |title=The importance of extracellular carbohydrate productionby marine epipelic diatoms |date=2003-01-01 |volume=40 |pages=183–240 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0065229605400051 |access-date=2024-04-04 |publisher=Academic Press |last2=Paterson |first2=David M.|series=Advances in Botanical Research |doi=10.1016/S0065-2296(05)40005-1 |isbn=978-0-12-005940-9 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The EPS produced by [[microalgae]] also enhance biofilm growth and help other members of the biofilm with adhesion and migration.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lundkvist |first1=M. |last2=Gangelhof |first2=U. |last3=Lunding |first3=J. |last4=Flindt |first4=M. R. |date=2007-11-01 |title=Production and fate of extracellular polymeric substances produced by benthic diatoms and bacteria: A laboratory study |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0272771407002004 |journal=Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science |series=Hydrodynamic control of aquatic ecosystem processes |volume=75 |issue=3 |pages=337–346 |doi=10.1016/j.ecss.2007.04.034 |bibcode=2007ECSS...75..337L |issn=0272-7714|url-access=subscription }}</ref> EPS are mostly composed of polysaccharides, but may also include [[protein]]s, [[nucleic acid]]s, [[lipid]]s, and low-molecular-weight, non-carbohydrate compounds.<ref name=":7" />

=== Seasonal variation ===
Intertidal biofilms exhibit [[Stratification (water)|stratification]], where different microorganisms arrange themselves in layers based on factors like [[seasonality]]. Microalgae are found on the lower shore<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal |last=Aleem |first=A |date=1950 |title=Distribution and Ecology of British Marine Littoral Diatoms |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2256526 |journal=[[British Ecology Society]] |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=75–106 |doi=10.2307/2256526 |jstor=2256526 |bibcode=1950JEcol..38...75A |url-access=subscription }}</ref> but their distribution can change. During the winter, a greater abundance and biomass of microalgae are found on the upper shore compared to the lower shore.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Thompson |first1=R. C. |last2=Norton |first2=T. A. |last3=Hawkins |first3=S. J. |date=2004 |title=Physical Stress and Biological Control Regulate the Producer-Consumer Balance in Intertidal Biofilms |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3450178 |journal=Ecology |volume=85 |issue=5 |pages=1372–1382 |doi=10.1890/03-0279 |jstor=3450178 |bibcode=2004Ecol...85.1372T |issn=0012-9658|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Seasonal variability is also observed in the relative abundance of microalgae in intertidal biofilms. Specifically, microalgae in tropical and temperate intertidal biofilms are most abundant during winter and spring, with abundance decreasing in the warmer months.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hill |first1=A. S. |last2=Hawkins |first2=S. J. |date=2009-05-11 |title=Seasonal And Spatial Variation of Epilithic Micro Algal Distribution and Abundance and its Ingestion By Patella Vulgata on A Moderately Exposed Rocky Shore |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-marine-biological-association-of-the-united-kingdom/article/abs/seasonal-and-spatial-variation-of-epilithic-micro-algal-distribution-and-abundance-and-its-ingestion-by-patella-vulgata-on-a-moderately-exposed-rocky-shore/36996ED62DA1E4C1A7DA039656DB767C |journal=Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom |language=en |volume=71 |issue=2 |pages=403–423 |doi=10.1017/S0025315400051675 |issn=1469-7769|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Cyanobacteria are relatively less affected by seasonal variation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mak |first1=Y. M |last2=Williams |first2=Gray A |date=1999-01-31 |title=Littorinids control high intertidal biofilm abundance on tropical, Hong Kong rocky shores |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022098198001221 |journal=Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology |volume=233 |issue=1 |pages=81–94 |doi=10.1016/S0022-0981(98)00122-1 |bibcode=1999JEMBE.233...81M |issn=0022-0981|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This may be attributed to their greater tolerance to stressors such as temperature and insolation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yadav |first1=Priya |last2=Singh |first2=Rahul Prasad |last3=Rana |first3=Shashank |last4=Joshi |first4=Diksha |last5=Kumar |first5=Dharmendra |last6=Bhardwaj |first6=Nikunj |last7=Gupta |first7=Rajan Kumar |last8=Kumar |first8=Ajay |date=2022-12-09 |title=Mechanisms of Stress Tolerance in Cyanobacteria under Extreme Conditions |journal=Stresses |language=en |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=531–549 |doi=10.3390/stresses2040036 |doi-access=free |issn=2673-7140}}</ref>

== Interactions within the biofilm ==
Interactions within biofilms are bidirectional. They can be affected by [[Negative feedback|negative]] and [[Positive feedback|positive feedback loops]], as well as indirect effects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Worm |first1=Boris |last2=Duffy |first2=J.Emmett |date=2003-12-01 |title=Biodiversity, productivity and stability in real food webs |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tree.2003.09.003 |journal=Trends in Ecology & Evolution |volume=18 |issue=12 |pages=628–632 |doi=10.1016/j.tree.2003.09.003 |issn=0169-5347|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These interactions contribute to the resilience and adaptability of intertidal biofilms.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Paine |first=R. T. |date=1969-01-15 |title=A Note on Trophic Complexity and Community Stability |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/282586 |journal=The American Naturalist |language=en |volume=103 |issue=929 |pages=91–93 |doi=10.1086/282586 |issn=0003-0147|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Trophic interactions ===
Within intertidal biofilms, [[Trophic level|trophic]] interactions exist between microphytobenthos and bacteria.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Hubas |first1=Cédric |chapter=Microphytobenthic Biofilms: Composition and Interactions |date=2018 |title=Mudflat Ecology |pages=63–90 |editor-last=Beninger |editor-first=Peter G. |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-99194-8_4 |access-date=2024-04-04 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-99194-8_4 |isbn=978-3-319-99194-8 |last2=Passarelli |first2=Claire |last3=Paterson |first3=David M.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> EPS, which are produced by microphytobenthos, act as a trophic resource, but their large size makes them difficult to break down and assimilate.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hoppe |first=Hans-Georg |date=1983 |title=Significance of exoenzymatic activities in the ecology of brackish water: measurements by means of methylumbelliferyl-substrates |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/44634717 |journal=Marine Ecology Progress Series |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=299–308 |doi=10.3354/meps011299 |jstor=44634717 |bibcode=1983MEPS...11..299H |issn=0171-8630}}</ref>  Bacteria secrete various enzymes like [[Β-Glucosidase|β-glucosidase]] to break down complex carbohydrate compounds in EPS.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Mckew |last2=Dumbrell |last3=Taylor |last4=McGenity |last5=Underwood |date=2013-06-01 |title=Differences between aerobic and anaerobic degradation of microphytobenthic biofilm-derived organic matter within intertidal sediments |url=https://academic.oup.com/femsec/article/84/3/495/578755 |access-date=2024-04-04 |website=academic.oup.com}}</ref> These carbohydrates serve as a nutrient source for heterotrophic bacteria and [[Sulfate-reducing bacteria|sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB)]],<ref name=":1" /> as well as a carbon source for consumers such as marine invertebrates.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Herman |first1=Peter M. J. |last2=Middelburg |first2=Jack J. |last3=Widdows |first3=John |last4=Lucas |first4=Cathy H. |last5=Heip |first5=Carlo H. R. |date=2000-10-05 |title=Stable isotopes as trophic tracers: combining field sampling and manipulative labelling of food resources for macrobenthos |url=https://www.int-res.com/abstracts/meps/v204/p79-92/ |journal=Marine Ecology Progress Series |language=en |volume=204 |pages=79–92 |doi=10.3354/meps204079 |bibcode=2000MEPS..204...79H |issn=0171-8630|hdl=20.500.11755/fca6f05f-4073-4cc1-86c8-54817f0edf5b |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Quorum Sensing (QS) ===
Biofilm communities facilitate both intra-species communication and inter-species communication through QS, which relies on the production and release of signaling molecules known as [[autoinducer]]s.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Bassler |first1=Bonnie L. |last2=Losick |first2=Richard |date=2006-04-21 |title=Bacterially Speaking |journal=Cell |volume=125 |issue=2 |pages=237–246 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2006.04.001 |issn=0092-8674|doi-access=free |pmid=16630813 }}</ref> When autoinducers reach a specific threshold concentration, signaling pathways are activated, resulting in physiological changes.<ref name=":1" /> QS, alongside other methods of cell signaling regulation, is important for intertidal biofilms, as it allows them to survive in fluctuating environments and varying conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Montgomery |first1=Kate |last2=Charlesworth |first2=James C. |last3=LeBard |first3=Rebecca |last4=Visscher |first4=Pieter T. |last5=Burns |first5=Brendan P. |date=2013-01-29 |title=Quorum Sensing in Extreme Environments |journal=Life  |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=131–148 |doi=10.3390/life3010131 |doi-access=free |issn=2075-1729 |pmc=4187201 |pmid=25371335|bibcode=2013Life....3..131M }}</ref> This is because the expression of many genes in biofilms is shown to be density-dependent, with QS playing a crucial role in modulating feedback loops.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Waters |first1=Christopher M. |last2=Bassler |first2=Bonnie L. |date=2005-11-01 |title=Quorum Sensing: Cell-to-Cell Communication in Bacteria |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.cellbio.21.012704.131001 |journal=Annual Review of Cell and Developmental Biology |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=319–346 |doi=10.1146/annurev.cellbio.21.012704.131001 |pmid=16212498 |issn=1081-0706|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Autoinducer signals have also resulted in biofilms having a very different architecture compared to those with no QS capabilities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Davies |first1=D. G. |last2=Parsek |first2=M. R. |last3=Pearson |first3=J. P. |last4=Iglewski |first4=B. H. |last5=Costerton |first5=J. W. |last6=Greenberg |first6=E. P. |date=1998-04-10 |title=The involvement of cell-to-cell signals in the development of a bacterial biofilm |journal=Science |volume=280 |issue=5361 |pages=295–298 |doi=10.1126/science.280.5361.295 |issn=0036-8075 |pmid=9535661|bibcode=1998Sci...280..295D }}</ref>
[[File:Mature biofilm structure.png|thumb|'''Various types of interactions within the biofilm'''(1) Communication through quorum sensing (2) Adaptations to varying conditions such as light]]

== Adaptations to varying conditions ==
Intertidal biofilms exhibit diverse adaptation mechanisms to cope with fluctuating conditions such as light stress, [[metal ion]] and [[oxidative stress]], and desiccation stress.

=== Light stress ===
As intertidal biofilms are found in locations with fluctuating environmental conditions, biofilm microalgae are often damaged by the accumulation of [[Reactive oxygen species|reactive oxygen species (ROS)]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Roncarati |first1=F. |last2=Rijstenbil |first2=J. == Ecological impact and functions ==
The cohesive nature of EPS contributes not only to the sediment's stability, preventing its resuspension under erosion, but also enhances [[flocculation]] processes. Flocculation processes involve the accumulation of fine sediments into larger flocs, modifying [[Biogeochemistry|biogeochemical exchanges]]. This stabilization is important for [[Geomorphology|geomorphologic]] evolution and the ecosystem health of coastal areas.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Jiasheng |last2=Chen |first2=Xindi |last3=Townend |first3=Ian |last4=Shi |first4=Benwei |last5=Du |first5=Jiabi |last6=Gao |first6=Jianhua |last7=Chuai |first7=Xiaowei |last8=Gong |first8=Zheng |last9=Wang |first9=Ya Ping |date=2021-04-01 |title=A comparison study on the sediment flocculation process between a bare tidal flat and a clam aquaculture mudflat: The important role of sediment concentration and biological processes |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0025322721000256 |journal=Marine Geology |volume=434 |article-number=106443 |doi=10.1016/j.margeo.2021.106443 |bibcode=2021MGeol.43406443L |issn=0025-3227|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A study from [[Jiangsu|Jiangsu coast, China]] concluded that flocculation processes affect the density, particle size, and settling velocity of suspended particles, which are essential for [[sedimentation]] and sediment transport.<ref name=":13" /> These processes are also important in biogeochemical cycles for nutrients and heavy metals due to the [[adsorption]] ability and transport function of particles in flocs.<ref name=":13" />

Intertidal marine biofilms on rocky substrates significantly impact estuarine carbon and nutrient dynamics. Biofilms in the [[Douro|Douro River]] estuary were observed to engage actively in biogeochemical processes, showing considerable [[net primary production]] that greatly exceeded respiration rates.<ref name=":11" /> These biofilms play a key role in nutrient fluxes, consistently removing [[nitrate]] and [[silicate]] from the water column while exhibiting variable fluxes of [[ammonium]] depending on light conditions, indicating a preference for ammonium assimilation by primary producers within the biofilms. Despite their limited spatial coverage, rocky biofilms account for a significant portion of the nitrate and silicate uptake compared to adjacent sandy and muddy sediments within the estuary.<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal |last=Bordalo |first=Adriano |date=2003-01-01 |title=Intertidal biofilms on rocky substratum can play a major role in estuarine carbon and nutrient dynamics |url=https://www.academia.edu/65673535 |journal=Marine Ecology Progress|volume=258 |page=275 |doi=10.3354/meps258275 |bibcode=2003MEPS..258..275M }}</ref>

== Impacts of anthropogenic activities ==

=== Biofouling on marine structures ===
The attachment and growth of marine organisms on submerged artificial structures, such as ship hulls and [[aquaculture]] infrastructures, can cause ecological and economic issues. This [[biofouling]] leads to increased drag resistance, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions for ships. It also restricts water exchange, raises disease risk, and causes deformation in aquaculture setups.<ref name=":12" />

=== Introduction of Non-Indigenous Species (NIS) ===
Biofouling on ships, both as hull fouling and through solid [[ballast]] (sand, rocks, and soil), is a major pathway for the arrival of NIS into new regions.<ref name=":12" /> This introduces significant risks to receiving ecosystems, potentially resulting in significant economic and ecological impacts. Ports, which are primary receivers of maritime trade goods, are particularly at high risk for NIS introductions.<ref name=":12" /> Monitoring NIS presence and impacts, while implementing preventive measures to minimize their settlement, are critical for marine environmental management.

=== Resilience of biofilms on human activities ===
A research study conducted along the southeast coast of [[Brazil]] showed that human activities, such as [[trampling]], were minimal. A trend of increased variability in biofilm biomass was observed with more intense trampling but no significant differences were found across trampling frequencies and intensities. The microorganisms' small size, which prevents complete removal by trampling, and the biofilms' capacity for rapid recovery may contribute to their high resilience to physical disturbance.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Leite |first1=Lucas G. |last2=Ciotti |first2=Áurea M. |last3=Christofoletti |first3=Ronaldo A. |date=2012-08-01 |title=Abundance of biofilm on intertidal rocky shores: Can trampling by humans be a negative influence? |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0141113612001122 |journal=Marine Environmental Research |volume=79 |pages=111–115 |doi=10.1016/j.marenvres.2012.06.001 |pmid=22738760 |bibcode=2012MarER..79..111L |issn=0141-1136|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

extract: An intertidal bioflim is a biofilm that forms on the intertidal region of bodies of water. Bacteria and various microorganisms, including algae and fungi, form communities of adhered cells called biofilms. A matrix of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) within the biofilm forms sticky coatings on individual sediment particles and detrital surfaces. This feature protects bacteria against environmental stresses like temperature and pH fluctuations, UV exposure, changes in salinity, depletion of nutrients, antimicrobial agents, desiccation, and predation. Particularly, in the ever-changing environments of intertidal systems, biofilms can facilitate a range of microbial processes and create protective microenvironments where cells communicate with each other and regulate further biofilm formation via Quorum Sensing (QS).,  While biofilm formation is advantageous to bacteria and other microorganisms involved, the attachment of microorganisms to ship hulls can increase fuel consumption and emission of greenhouse gases, as well as introduce Non-Indigenous Species (NIS), potentially resulting in harmful economic and ecological impacts on the receiving ecosystems.
